paras: The Lewisville cabin shooting and rapes took place on the night of June 4, 1882, near Lewisville, Texas, when a group of armed men shot into the cabin of Perry Bolin, a Black man, forced their way in and raped two Black women. The accusation surfaced at a hearing on a separate complaint by two farmers whom the same men had shot at that night, and officers were reported to be pursuing the three accused.

According to a special dispatch to the Dallas Daily Herald dated June 5, Joe Dawson and Add Crow, described as "respectable farmers," were shot at six or seven times near Timber Creek while returning home. They said they recognized the voice and dress of Will McCombs jr. and filed a complaint the next morning against him and against Austin and Harden Lott. The Lott brothers proved an alibi and were discharged, while "a strong case" was made against McCombs, Jim Furgerson and Ambres Stevenson.

The evidence at that hearing also indicated that the same men had gone to the home of Perry Bolin, who lived on W. A. Gulledge's place, shot into his cabin several times, forced themselves in and raped two Black women. Gulledge, hearing the shots, went to the rescue of his tenants but was "ridiculed, intimidated and forced to retreat" by the men, who were "well armed with liquor and weapons."

The accused were not in custody when the dispatch was sent, and officers were said to be in pursuit. No report of an arrest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage, and the two women are not named.

The Dallas Daily Herald ran the item on June 6 as a brief local special headed only "Lewisville." The same day the Omaha Daily Bee printed a wire version in its crime column under "Texas Jayhawkers," a heading that framed the episode around the attempt to "jayhawk two respectable farmers" rather than the attack on the Black household. Neither paper commented on the rapes beyond the single sentence reporting them, and no further coverage was found.

The Omaha version named the third accused man as Ambrose Rudd rather than Ambres Stevenson and said Gulledge's tenants, not Gulledge, were forced "to treat the boys"; the Dallas text, the local special, is the more coherent of the two.

reader.title: Lewisville cabin shooting and rapes (1882)
bases: A small armed group shot into a Black tenant's cabin, forced its way in and was charged with raping two Black women; no one was reported killed (A1, A2).
Both reports carry the same Lewisville dispatch of June 5 in nearly identical words, so they are one source rather than two independent accounts (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Lewisville correspondent (evidence at the hearing)
accounts.gist: Evidence at the hearing on the farmers' complaint indicated that the same men shot into Perry Bolin's cabin, forced their way in and raped two Black women, then drove off Gulledge; officers were in pursuit.

framing.detail: The Dallas Herald gave a plain local special headed only 'Lewisville', calling the shot-at men 'respectable farmers' and the accused 'the boys'.
The Omaha Bee ran the dispatch under 'Texas Jayhawkers' in a crime-news column, with the deck 'Texas Jayhawker's Pulling Premiscuously on Peaceable Citizens'.
